oneliner.t: First-term Democratic U.S. senator from Atlanta, a former congressional staffer and investigative-documentary executive, who won the January 2021 runoff over David Perdue and is seeking a second term against Republican Rep. Mike Collins.

hometown.t: Atlanta (grew up in Northlake, DeKalb County, metro Atlanta)

upbringing.t: Thomas Jonathan Ossoff grew up in the Northlake area of metro Atlanta. His mother, Heather Fenton, immigrated from Sydney, Australia, worked as a management consultant and co-founded NewPower PAC, which backs women running for local office in Georgia; his father, Richard Ossoff, is an attorney who owns Strafford Publications. He converted to Judaism before his bar mitzvah and grew up among relatives who survived the Holocaust. He went to the private Paideia School, and as a high-school student he interned for Rep. John Lewis. He previously held dual Australian citizenship through his mother.

education.school: Georgetown University, Walsh School of Foreign Service

career.role: National-security staffer and legislative assistant for foreign affairs and defense
Managing director and CEO; co-funded the firm with $250,000 of an inheritance
career.org: Insight: The World Investigates (TWI), London-based investigative documentary producer (BBC and other outlets)

career.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia (sworn in Jan. 20, 2021)

platform.t: Says his campaigns refuse corporate-PAC and federal-lobbyist money, backs banning corporate PACs, and sponsored a bill to bar members of Congress (and spouses) from trading stocks.
Blames Trump's tariffs, which he says Collins backed, for higher grocery and fuel costs; said Democrats would repeal them.
Calls the 2026 Iran war a 'disaster' that raised gas and diesel prices; voted in March 2026 for a war-powers resolution limiting presidential force against Iran.
Attacks the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid cuts and the expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies; campaign site says he works to expand Medicaid and protect Social Security and Medicare.
Says Americans deserve secure borders; was one of 12 Senate Democrats who voted for the Laken Riley Act in January 2025; criticizes job-site raids.
Said in the Oct. 8 debate that Georgia's voter-ID law is good; does not support the federal SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement.
Calls the U.S.–Israel relationship 'ironclad' but says support should not be unconditional; has voted both for and against Sanders resolutions to block arms sales.
Centers his first general-election ad on his bipartisan investigation of abuse in Georgia's foster-care system and his child-sex-trafficking legislation.

promises.t: Ban stock trading by members of Congress.
Ban corporate PACs (legislation introduced, per campaign).
Repeal Trump's tariffs (stated as a Democratic goal in the Oct. 8 debate).
Work to end the war with Iran.

record.t: Born Feb. 16, 1987, in Atlanta; grew up in Northlake in metro Atlanta.

claims.claim: Was an investigative journalist whose small business produced award-winning investigations of corruption and war crimes for international news organizations.

record.t: CEO of London-based Insight TWI 2013–2021, which produced BBC investigations into ISIS war crimes and East African death squads. Awards for its work were not independently checked.

claims.claim: His campaigns refuse contributions from corporate PACs and federal lobbyists.

record.t: Donor-side FEC data show several corporate PAC gifts were refunded (Truist $5,000 in 2021; Dell $5,000 in 2025; Citizens Financial $2,500 in 2026), consistent with the policy. But a $1,500 Lumen Technologies PAC gift (May 27, 2026) shows no refund in the data, and the campaign took about $99,500 from trade-association PACs in 2025–26 (e.g., Mortgage Bankers, National Association of Broadcasters, American Hotel & Lodging, agricultural groups). Those are industry PACs, though not single-company PACs. Individual federal-lobbyist donations were not checked.

claims.claim: Sponsored a bill to ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

record.t: Introduced legislation in January 2022 to bar members of Congress and their spouses from trading stocks. It has not become law; a Senate cloture vote on a different stock-trading bill (H.R. 7008) failed Sept. 30, 2026.

claims.claim: Helped pass a congressional stock-trading ban through a major Senate committee for the first time.

record.t: No committee markup record or news report of this was opened during research; needs a congress.gov check.

claims.claim: In the Senate he exposed abuse of children in Georgia's foster care system.

record.t: The AJC describes a bipartisan Ossoff investigation into abuse in Georgia's foster-care system, but only in reporting on his own ad; the subcommittee report itself was not opened.

claims.claim: Exposed civil-rights abuses in the federal prison system and mistreatment of military families by private housing contractors.

record.t: Wikipedia references a bipartisan investigation he led into medical mistreatment of women in U.S. detention (Nov. 2022). The specific prison and military-housing reports were not opened.

claims.claim: Studied diplomacy at Georgetown and earned a Master of Science from the London School of Economics.

record.t: B.S., Georgetown School of Foreign Service, 2009; master's in international political economy, LSE, 2013.

claims.claim: Mentored by civil-rights leader and Congressman John Lewis.

record.t: Interned for Lewis in high school; Lewis recommended him for his job with Rep. Hank Johnson.

claims.claim: Lives in Atlanta with his wife, Dr. Alisha Kramer, and their daughters.

record.t: Married Alisha Kramer, an Emory OB-GYN, in 2017; two daughters (born 2021 and 2025).

claims.claim: Worked to upgrade infrastructure and expand high-speed internet statewide, including $1.3 billion.

record.t: He voted for the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The $1.3 billion figure and his role in it were not traced to a source opened during research.

claims.claim: Ad 'This Is Mike Collins': Collins 'admitted' that President Trump is in the Epstein files.

said.where: Ossoff TV/digital ad 'This Is Mike Collins'

record.t: PolitiFact rated it Mostly False. Collins did say he was sure Trump was in the files, but the ad cuts his explanation that Trump appears because he alerted the FBI and banned Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, not because of wrongdoing.

claims.claim: Ad 'The Vote': Collins 'voted to cover up the Epstein files' on July 15, 2025, even after it was learned girls as young as 14 were abused.

record.t: Reporting confirms the ad cites a July 15, 2025 vote and that Collins later reversed his stance on releasing the files. The House roll call itself (and whether it was a procedural vote) was not opened, and no independent fact-check was found. 'Cover up' is a characterization.

said.t: Introduced a bill to ban members of Congress and spouses from trading stocks.

did.t: His latest annual disclosure (as summarized by Quiver) shows his holdings in a qualified blind trust set up in 2021 plus cash and two funds; no individual stock trades are reported.

said.t: Says his campaigns refuse corporate-PAC and federal-lobbyist contributions.

did.t: Several corporate PAC gifts were refunded, but trade-association PACs gave about $99,500 in 2025–26 and one 2026 corporate PAC gift (Lumen, $1,500) shows no refund in the data.

said.t: Calls U.S.–Israel ties 'ironclad' but does not support unconditional aid.

did.t: Mixed record on Sanders resolutions: supported blocking arms (Nov. 2024), opposed two resolutions (Apr. 2025), voted to block a rifle sale (July 2025).
Voted for the Laken Riley Act, one of 12 Democrats to do so.

promises_prev.promise: Ban stock trading by members of Congress and their spouses (bill introduced January 2022).

evidence.t: He introduced the ban in 2022; no congressional stock-trading ban has become law. On Sept. 30, 2026, the Senate rejected cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act.

complicating.t: H.R. 7008 is a different bill from his; how he voted on that cloture motion was not checked here (covered in Sophia's separate key-vote file). His campaign says a ban cleared a Senate committee for the first time, which was not verified.

entries.t: Led 25 Democratic senators in calling for an immediate ceasefire in the May 2021 Gaza conflict.
One of 19 senators to support Sanders resolutions blocking military aid/arms sales to Israel (Nov. 20, 2024).
Voted against a pair of Sanders resolutions to block offensive arms sales (April 2025); voted to block a sale of 20,000 automatic rifles (July 2025).
Voted in March 2026 for a war-powers resolution limiting force against Iran without authorization; in October called the war a 'disaster' that raised fuel prices.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft).
Says borders must be secure; opposes job-site raids.

Describes U.S. support for Israel as 'ironclad' but not unconditional; the Atlanta Jewish Times publisher challenged that in an open letter, and the campaign did not comment.

note.t: Per Quiver's summary of his annual Senate report (published Sept. 16, 2025): the largest asset is 'The Thomas Jonathan Ossoff Qualified Blind Trust of 2021' (up to $5M), plus a Fidelity government money-market fund (up to $100K), Wells Fargo cash (up to $50K), and two funds, Parnassus Core Equity and Vanguard ESG International (up to $15K each). The net-worth range uses the standard disclosure bands under those 'up to' values; liabilities were not reported in the summary. The original eFD filing was not opened. Quiver separately estimates about $3.2M. No individual stock trades are reported because holdings sit in a qualified blind trust.

committees: Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (listed for 117th Congress)

democracy.t: In the first debate, said Georgia's voter-ID law is good and accused Collins and Trump of remaining fixated on overturning the 2020 election.

note.t: Born and raised in metro Atlanta (1987) and lives in Atlanta. He studied in Washington, D.C. and London and ran a London-based company from 2013 to 2021; where he lived during those years isn't documented here, so 39 years counts his lifetime ties, not continuous residence.

checks.legal: Courts: CourtListener and Justia could not be reached from this research tool (fetch blocked without approval), so courts are 'news'. Wikipedia and 2025–26 race coverage (AJC, Axios, Georgia Recorder, WSB, FOX 5, ANF) report no lawsuits or charges against him. Ethics: no Senate Ethics Committee matter appears in Wikipedia or race coverage; the Senate Ethics site was not searched directly.
checks.foreign: FARA: exact-name check of DOJ FARA bulk files (registrants, short forms, foreign principals), run 2026-10-13, found no match. Disclosures: 2017 House candidate report on file; current Senate holdings reviewed only through Quiver's summary (blind trust, U.S. funds; no foreign assets noted). Previously held dual Australian citizenship through his mother (Wikipedia). TWI was a London company that produced for the BBC; no foreign-government client is documented.
checks.claims: Mechanical v2.1 sample: (a) every checkable factual claim on electjon.com/bio (10 rated; 'fighting for' or 'worked to' items such as $35 insulin, HBCU funding, job training and Medicaid expansion were treated as advocacy, not checkable outcomes); (b) the campaign site has no issues/platform page (navigation: Home, About Jon, News, Shop, Volunteer), so this part is empty; (c) ad spend is unknown, so the two most-covered 2026 Ossoff ads were used: 'This Is Mike Collins' (June 17, 2026; PolitiFact) and 'The Vote' (July 2026; seven-figure buy; FOX 5, Daily Signal). Outside the sample and not rated: his statement that Collins is 'under federal investigation for illegal misuse of tax dollars' (a House Ethics review after an OCC referral; no finding yet) and his Aug. 16, 2026 claim that Collins is one of Congress's most active crypto traders (PolitiFact: True).
checks.democracy: Certification roll calls (2005, 2017, 2021; 6 read from Sophia records): he does not appear because he was sworn in Jan. 20, 2021, after the count. Searched Wikipedia and debate coverage for statements on 2020/2024 results.

recordx.note: Not available: GovTrack missed-vote %, Senate eFD filing dates (efdsearch.senate.gov was not opened; Quiver shows an annual report was public by Sept. 2025), and the FEC committee RFAI/notices tab. None of these could be confirmed, so recordx is incomplete.

corp.t: Despite a no-corporate-PAC pledge, FEC donor-side records show about $99,500 from business trade-association PACs in 2025–26 (Mortgage Bankers, Broadcasters, Hotel & Lodging, SIFMA, insurance and farm groups) plus $6,750 coded corporate. Several single-company PAC gifts were refunded; a $1,500 Lumen PAC gift (May 2026) shows no refund. Labor PACs gave $210,158 in 2025–26.

lobby.t: Pro-Israel PAC money: J Street PAC $21,789 career (mostly earmarked; $19,969 in 2025–26), JACPAC $14,030 (2017–2022), and $102,267 in DMFI PAC independent expenditures supporting him (2021–22 period). Also $2,000 from the Nigerian Diaspora Political Affairs Committee (2020). No AIPAC PAC or United Democracy Project money found.

research_notes: MONEY: the 2026 FEC figures cover the 2025–26 two-year period only (receipts $77.28M). Wikipedia's $97.99M 'raised as of June 30, 2026' is the six-year Senate-term total (2021–26), which matches the sum of the 2022, 2024 and 2026 periods here. 'other' ($8.58M) = receipts minus individuals, PACs and party, likely joint-fundraising transfers (not itemized here). pac_biz (corporate $6,750, trade $99,500, co-op $1,000, labor $210,158) and pac_ideo (leadership $400,500, membership $108,683, ideological $80,708, super PAC/hybrid $74,750, candidate $8,000) come from donor-side reports, so they sum to about $990K versus $920K reported by the campaign; J Street earmarks are inside 'membership'. Small/large individual split, industries, top individual donors and in-state % were not retrieved (OpenSecrets not opened). Q3 2026 report due Oct. 15 is not included. Q2-26 $20M is the campaign's figure via the Augusta Press. OUTSIDE: Schedule E data through early Oct. 2026; AJC reports SLF committed $44M and One Nation $15M against him, and Senate Majority PAC announced a $20M buy for him (ANF, May 18, 2026; article not opened). Super PAC donor lists not retrieved. NOT FOUND/NOT CHECKED: Senate eFD originals, GovTrack missed votes, sponsored/enacted bill counts, Heritage/other scorecards, AIPAC's own endorsement page, Track AIPAC (not reachable without search result), Senate Ethics site, CourtListener. Wikipedia mentions a Sept. 2025 'stolen valor' dispute in the race without detail; not researched. Photo omitted (no confirmed file URL). The Atlanta Press Club debate (Oct. 13, 2026) took place per his campaign's Oct. 14 release; a third debate Ossoff proposed in July was not documented.
